(p-69) Sūrat ash-Shams (Surah of the Sun) – its purpose:

Affirmation of His, glory be to Him and exalted, control over souls, which are the lamps of bodies, leading them toward happiness, or toward deceit, humiliation and wretchedness. Just as the sun is the lamp of the sphere, so He, glory be to Him, disposes souls by choice, misguiding, guiding, bestowing bliss and misery.

His, glory be to Him, control over the sun is of the same kind: [it brings] health and sickness, order and disorder; and likewise over all of creation, with His great majesty. Its name, ash-Shams (the Sun), clearly indicates this when one reflects on the oath [and what is sworn to] by what He made known and alluded to: "Bismillāh" [Who is] the Supreme King, so to Him belongs universal control; "ar-Raḥmān," whose mercy embraces everything, so to Him belongs bestowal of blessings; "ar-Raḥīm," who singles out whom He wills for success, and so perfects His blessing upon them.

* *

When he established in Sūrat al-Balad that man is in toil (kabad), and concluded it by saying that whoever deviates from His path is in the most wretched wretchedness, which is the Fire closed over them, he swore at the beginning of this [surah] that the one who does this, first and last, is Allah, glory be to Him, [because] He comes between a person and his heart and between the heart and its reason. So He said, swearing by what indicates the completeness of His knowledge (p-70) and the all-encompassing scope of His power over the horizons, upper and lower, and over souls, the blessed and the wretched. He began with the upper world, which conveys with certainty the knowledge that He is the free, choosing Agent, and the knowledge of the necessity of His essence and the perfection of His attributes, and that is the highest degree of the theoretical faculties, as a reminder of the greatness of His bounties, so as to move one to be utterly absorbed in thanking Him for His blessings, which is the ultimate [perfection] of the practical faculties. Moreover, the first thing sworn by reminds of what the last of those [verses] ended with, of the Fire: ﴿By the sun﴾, i.e., gathering together benefit and harm by its light and heat, just as the intellects are likewise: none is brighter when they blaze, nor darker when they perish. ﴿And its brightness﴾, i.e., its light arising from its great and wondrously created body, which reminds of fires when they shine and their dominion is established, like the shining of the lights of the intellects. Ḍuḥā, with a ḍammah and without the long vowel: the early part of the day when it rises high; with a fatḥah and the long vowel: the intensity of heat [after the day has extended]; and a thing is ḍāḥin when it is exposed to the sun and heat.

Since he opened with mention of the sign of the day, he followed it with mention of the sign of the night, saying: ﴿And by the moon﴾, i.e., the one that acquires its light from the sun, just as the lights of souls derive from the lights of intellects; ﴿when it follows it﴾, i.e., follows it (the sun) in its circuit and in its light, by which is indicated that its light comes from the sun's light, through its nearness that obliterates its own light and its distance by which it acquires light in proportion to the part of its body that faces the sun. It continues to increase until the facing is complete, and so its light is complete on the night of full moon (p-71) when the two are in opposition at the horizon of the east and the west. From there it begins to approach (the sun), and it wanes by the degree to which it deviates from the opposition. The attribution of "following" to it is figurative, applied in relation to what the moon looks toward from it in this way.

When he had mentioned the two verses, he mentioned what they are signs of, and he began with them because there is no well-being for him except through them, just as there is no well-being for the body except through the soul and the intellect. So he said: ﴿By the day﴾, i.e., by that which is the place of dispersal within what the decrees have run, ﴿when it displays it﴾, i.e., when it displays the sun with a great adornment, some of which is greater than others in terms of length and shortness, clearness and cloudiness, mist and clarity and turbidity. Just as bodies sometimes purify the hearts, souls and intellects, and sometimes defile them, because the intellect is at the height of clarity and calls to good in childhood, and then it continues to increase and decrease according to the purity of the body in good disposition, or its impurity through bad disposition, until the person becomes pure light, a speaking angel, when the body conforms to the intellect and they cooperate in good. Or he becomes pure darkness, an accursed devil, when the body opposes the intellect through bad disposition and wickedness of nature.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 91, verse 4:

When he had mentioned the source of light, he mentioned the place of darkness, saying: ﴿By the night﴾, i.e., which is the opposite of the day, so it is the place of stillness, contraction and concealment (p-72) ﴿when it covers it﴾, i.e., it covers the sun, so its light departs when it sets, and the shadows of the earth extend over its face that is turned toward us, so the eastern horizon begins to darken. That darkness extends according to the length and shortness of the night, just as the light of the intellect covers the body by means of its nature, through its wickedness and the baseness of its substance. All of this occurs in known measures and fixed balanced proportions, in which there is no disorder and to which no dissolution befalls, until the Lord of Majesty wills. He did not express it in the past tense as he did for the day, because the night does not remove the light all at once but gradually, bit by bit, and it is never free of some light, unlike the day. For when the day reveals the sun, and there is no cloud or haze, it makes the sun manifest in a single instant, so no darkness remains with it in any way.

And the heaven and He who built it. [Hmm—need faithful translation.]

Let me translate properly:

When he had mentioned the two verses and the place of their effect, he mentioned the place of all of them, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿By the heaven﴾, that is, the one which is the locus of all that and its manifestation, just as bodies are the locus of souls, and souls are the composite of intellects. When he elevated the thoughts from the greatest of the tangible sensible things, which are touched, to what is below it in sensation but above it in need of exercising thought, he ascended to the highest inner reality which is the intended one in itself, and it is the Originator of all that, expressing it by the particle used for what does not reason, along with the indication of the oath itself, that for Him is complete knowledge and the great comprehensiveness of the profound wisdom. This is an alert that they described Him with association and denial of the Resurrection, in that lowly station, and equating Him with the inanimate objects they worshipped, despite His attributes of perfection which no other has anything approaching any of them, as a rebuke to them through allusion and hint, and pointing to the intensity of the wonder at them, since it is the particle of wonder. So He said: ﴿And He who built it﴾, that is, this firmly constructed structure in which He assembled what He mentioned, as an indication of what lies beyond it, which description cannot reach.

"And [by] the earth, and how He spread it out (ṭaḥāhā)" — the verse reads: ﴿And the earth, and how He spread it out﴾. When he mentioned the building (al-binā'), he mentioned the cradle (al-mihād), so he said: ﴿And the earth﴾, [i.e.,] the one which is your bed (firāsh), is in the position of the places where you exercise your intellectual dispositions (taṣarrufāt) concerning the intended meanings. ﴿And how He spread it out (ṭaḥāhā)﴾, i.e., He spread it out in a manner in which it encompasses all living creatures, and is itself encompassed within the concave of the spheres (al-aflāk). Although it holds firm through power, it is as if it were tossed in the currents of its seas. It is the place of distance and destruction (al-bu'd wa'l-halāk) and the locus of gathering (al-jam'). All of this is indicated by the expression with this wording, pointing to what there is in the striving of man of the like of this. The people of insight (ahl al-baṣā'ir) said: there is nothing in the outer world (al-'ālam al-āfāqī) except that in the inner world (al-'ālam al-nafsānī) there is its counterpart. They recited on this:

*Your cure is within you, and you do not perceive it; / your disease is from you, and you deny it.*

*You think that you are a small part, / while within you the greatest world is folded up.*

So the heavens are seven, like the layers of the head (ṭibāq al-ra's), which are connected to the spiritual and sensory faculties (al-quwā al-ma'nawiyya wa'l-ḥissiyya), (p-74) such as the memory (al-dhākira), the retentive faculty (al-ḥāfiẓa), the estimative faculty (al-wāhima), the imaginative faculty (al-mukhayyila), the cogitative faculty (al-mufakkira), the common sense (al-ḥiss al-mushtarak), and that which is for the divider of sight in the eye. The counterpart of the sun is the spirit (al-rūḥ) in its radiance and beauty; the counterpart of the night is the nature (al-ṭab'), for whatever light it has is from the spirit, just as the night likewise has no light except from the sun, through its conveying [of light] to the luminous moon and the stars. The counterpart of the day, which is luminous in its origin but clouded by what is imagined for it of clouds and the like, is the heart (al-qalb), and its clouds are the doubts and psychic illusions (al-shukūk wa'l-awhām al-nafsiyya). The counterpart of the moon, in its darkness by origin and its illumination by the sun, is the soul (al-nafs); when the receiving heart acquires light from the spirit for it, it illuminates the whole body, and when it grows dark, the whole [body] grows dark. The inner organs are like the stars, by which the body stands, and it illuminates existence for it through the spirit and the soul. The rains are like tears, the heat like sorrow, the cold like joy, the thunder like speech, the lightning like the flash of insight, and the winds like the breath (al-nafs) — and other wonders [of this kind] for whoever reflects. The lower world (al-'ālam al-sufliyy) also has seven layers. Al-Malawī said: "Its counterpart is the layer of the skin," and it is three [layers]; [and] the layer of the flesh, the layer of the fat, (p-75) the layer of the veins, and the layer of the nerves. The mountains are like the bones, and the minerals (al-ma'ādin), among them are waters, and among them the sweet, like saliva; the salty, like tears; the bitter, as in the ear; and the foul-smelling, as in the nose. Among them is that which flows, like urine, and that which is like springs, which is blood. The torrent (al-sayl) is like sweat. The malleable minerals, like iron and lead, are the filth of the earth, and they are like excrement and what comes out of the skin of impurity. The plants are like hair: at times it is shaved (ka-al-ḥaṣād), and at times it is plucked out like plucking (ka-al-natf). The animals that are in it are like lice, and its birds like fleas. The populated body is what turns toward it, and its ruin is what turns away.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 91, verse 7:

When he had completed the allusion to the souls for the people of insight, he stated the matter plainly for those below them, so the Exalted said: ﴿And a soul﴾, meaning, any soul in which He, glorified is He, gathered the entire world. And since souls are the most wondrous and comprehensive of what exists in the cosmos, He expressed about them with ﴿and He proportioned it﴾ (al-taswiyah), urging contemplation of their affair, so that one may infer from them their Originator, and strive to set right their condition. So the Exalted said: ﴿and He proportioned it﴾, meaning, He balanced it according to this most perfect law in its organs, and in what it contains of substances, accidents and meanings, and the wondrous temperament of humours that are mutually discordant, which He harmonised through proportion and balance, making them intermingled (p-76). The context, the preceding and following verses indicate that the answer to the oath is implied, its estimate being: Indeed, the Glorified and Exalted has fashioned your souls with diverse natures, equipping them thereby for what He wills of hearts, of purification and corruption, through the power and choice He has granted you, and has most emphatically given you warning about purifying your souls and cleansing your hearts, by believing in the Resurrection with a proof clearer than the sun, free of doubt or confusion, so that you may be saved from the punishment of this world and the Hereafter by attaining piety and casting off wickedness and transgression.

And the Ustadh Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: Because His definition, exalted is He, of man through what He created in him of toil (kabad) was previously mentioned in Surat al-Balad, together with what He made for him, glorified is He, of instruments of sight, and spread out for him of proofs and lessons, and displayed in the form of one who possesses his reins, and distinguished his right guidance from his obstinacy: ﴿And We showed him the two paths﴾ [al-Balad: 10], ﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way﴾ [al-Insan: 3]. This is by means of the acquired power (al-qudrah al-kasbiyyah) that He gave him, whose reality is concern, or "why?" and "how?", and not autonomy and independence. Then ﴿And Allah created you and what you do﴾ [al-Saffat: 96]. In this surah, glorified and exalted is He, swore an oath concerning the success of the one who chose his right guidance, exerted his effort, and spent his wealth: ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies it﴾ [al-Shams: 9], and the ruin of the one whose guidance was lost, so he followed his desire: ﴿And he has certainly failed who instills it [with corruption]﴾ [al-Shams: 10]. Thus He clarified the condition of the two groups and the conduct of the two paths. End.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 91, verse 8:

When the most astonishing of its affairs was immorality (fujur), because He, glory be to Him, had made desires and appetites dominant over it, and it knows, by what the sound transmitted report (naql sahih) and the restraint of its reason ('aql) provide, that immorality is the most ugly of ugly things, and that God-consciousness (taqwa), because of the rational sovereignty ('aql malaki) and the luminous innate knowledge (gharizat al-'ilm al-nawrani) that He established over it, is the most beautiful of beautiful things, and it tastes that immorality is the most appealing of appealing things, and that God-consciousness is the bitterest, most difficult, heaviest and most exhausting of things, He said, informing that this is something no one other than it is able to do, because it is more astonishing than everything that came before, since the beast does not advance toward what harms it while it sees it, even if it is cut to pieces, whereas the human advances toward what harms him while he knows it and fights whoever prevents him from it. Then He said, giving the cause of what He omitted from the answer to the oath: ﴿Then He inspired it﴾, that is, the soul, with the inspiration of the primordial natural disposition (fitra) that preceded, the first (time), before, ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ [al-A'raf 7:172], ﴿its wickedness﴾, that is, its impulse toward inclining to the calls of desires and the absence of the fear that compels one to break through the fence of the Sharia (sacred law), by reason of that nature in which He balanced its essence and attributes, forcing mutually repellent things into blending, to the utmost degree of balance; ﴿and its God-consciousness﴾, that is, its fear, which made it necessary for it to remain still and to guard itself with the protections of the Sharia. So the verse is of the type of ihtibak (a device in which each of two opposites is mentioned and the other is implied): mention of immorality first indicates the stillness that is its opposite second, and mention of God-consciousness second indicates its opposite first, which is the absence of fear. Her inspiration with both matters means that He made her aware of good and evil, prepared and ready for each of them. Then He increased that with complete clarification, such that no ambiguity remained, so the doubts disappeared, rationally through innate disposition and inspiration, and through transmission through the message and the informing. He indicated by the idafa (possessive construction) that all of that is attributed to her and written upon her, even though it is by His creation and decree, because He deposited in her a power and made for her a choice suitable for each of the two paths, and He made clear the matter of the two paths in the Books and through the tongues of the Messengers, peace and blessings be upon them, after He had bestowed upon her the upright natural disposition and concealed from her the secret of the divine decree and power and the knowledge of the outcome. Thereby He established the proof against her and made the path clear.

Since it is known that whoever hears this speech knows that righteousness (taqwa) is only something commanded, and wickedness (fujur) is only something forbidden, and so he anticipates what is said about these two and what results from them, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He has succeeded﴾, meaning he attained all his aims, ﴿who purifies it﴾, meaning who developed it, set it right, and cleansed it with a great cleansing, through the beneficial knowledge and righteous deeds that Allah facilitates for him, and purified it by what Allah facilitates for him of keeping away from blameworthy traits, because each is made easy for what he was created for. And religion is built upon adornment (tahliya) and clearing away (takhliya), and "zakka" is suitable for both meanings.

﴿And he has failed﴾ means his aim is denied, of what He has prepared for others in the Hereafter, and he has lost, and his striving has been in vain. ﴿who buries it﴾ means he leads it astray with a great misguidance, corrupts it, defiles its life, degrades it, belittles it, and destroys it with the vile beliefs, the evil deeds, the foul intentions and states, and conceals it with ignorance, wickedness, boorishness and disobedience. The root of "dassaha" (buries/corrupts) is "dassa" (to hide). Purification (tazkiyah) means that a person is eager that his sun not be eclipsed, his moon not be darkened, his day not be clouded, and his night not be extinguished. Burying (tadsis) at its least means neglecting the matter until his sun is eclipsed, his moon is darkened, his day is clouded, and his night endures. The ways to this are to consider the counterparts of what has been mentioned among the spiritual realities (al-ruhaniyyat), and to give every possessor of a right his right. The counterpart of the sun is prophethood (nubuwwah), for it is entirely a dazzling light and an overpowering clarity. Its forenoon (duha) is messengership (risalah), and its moon is sainthood (wilayah). The day is gnosis (irfan), and the night is the soul's lack of tranquility through the remembrance of God and what has come from Him, and its turning away from submitting to accept what has come of prophethood or sainthood. The scholars who act upon their knowledge are the friends of God (awliya' Allah). The two imams Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "If the scholars are not the friends of God, then God has no friend." This was related from them both by the memorizer (al-Hafiz) Abu Bakr al-Khatib, and it is mentioned in al-Tibyan and other works of al-Nawawi. The counterpart of the sky is honour, elevation above desires, and above the steps of the devils, from among mankind and the jinn. The earth's counterpart is humility toward the right of God, His Messenger, and the believers, so that by its bringing forth benefits for them, it is like the earth bringing forth its plants. Burying is the opposite of this. Whoever does evil has degraded himself and belittled it, and so he conceals it, just as the base people (al-li'am) descend into the bottoms of valleys and their narrow passes, where their places are hidden from travelers, while the generous descend onto the hills and kindle fires for travelers, and make their places known to their guests, the dwellings of nobles on the frontiers, as it has been said:

A people whose visit is easy for the one in need,
but whose abode is steep for the horsemen.

As the context concerns warning (al-tarhib) through what Surat al-Balad indicates, and the mention of wickedness (al-fujur) is placed first here, and warning is more effective in urging purification (al-zaka'), He said, indicating the ruin of the one who corrupts (al-mudassi), so that whoever hears its report may take a lesson from it, especially if its effects are known: ﴿Thamud denied﴾. He made their action feminine because the effect of their denial was weak, since every hearer of it knows their wrongdoing in it, owing to the clarity of their sign and the ugliness of their outcome, and their lowness of aspirations and vileness of dispositions. He singled them out because their sign, although it was in itself the clearest of signs, was the most indicative of the Hour. Quraysh and the rest of the Arabs know of them, because they see their remains and transmit their reports ﴿by their transgression﴾, meaning that their denial of their Messenger, and of everything he brought from God the Exalted, was brought about by the attribute of transgression (al-tughyan) that was in their souls. Transgression is exceeding the measure, rising beyond it, excessiveness in disbelief, and extravagance in sins and wrongdoing. Or it means by what they were threatened with of the swift punishment, and it is the Ta'iyah (the overwhelming calamity) by which they were destroyed (p-٨١). The verb taghā is of the waw-ya' type (wawi yā'i); it is said: taghā, like da'ā, yatghū, tughwā and tughwānan, with its first vowel dammah, like tugha, yutgha; and taghiya, like radiya, taghyan and tughyānan, with kasrah and dammah. So al-tughwā, with a fatha, is a noun, and with a dammah it is a verbal noun (masdar). The yā' was changed into a wāw, on the assumption that it is a yā'-type verb, to distinguish between the noun and the attribute. The expression with it was chosen rather than the yā'-type form because of the strength of the wāw, so it conveys that they reached the utmost limit in their denial, and thus they were at the extreme of the evil of their punishment.

When he mentioned their denial, he indicated it by his saying: ﴿When﴾, meaning that their denial or their transgression became actual in deed, when ﴿the most wretched of them rose up﴾, meaning the most wretched of Thamud in misery, and this is the slayer of the she-camel, for sharing in the disbelief and for the addition of directly committing the hamstringing. He is Qidar ibn Salif. Or it is [and] whoever agreed with him upon her slaughter, for the superlative form (af'al al-tafdil), when it is put in the genitive construction (idafa), is suitable for both the singular and the plural.

﴿فَقالَ لَهُمْ﴾ That is, because of the rising up (of the one who hamstrung her) or the denial, which indicated their intent to harm her. He stated the noun explicitly and did not use a pronoun, and he specified the explicit mention by the Divine Name [as a sign] of the great significance of their sign and the wondrous nature of their beginning and their end. So he said: ﴿رَسُولُ اللَّهِ﴾ "the Messenger of Allah," that is, the King to whom all command belongs. Honouring him is therefore part of honouring the One who sent him, and he is Salih, upon him be peace. The same applies to the she-camel. He expressed it with "the Messenger" because his function is to convey and to warn, which is what is mentioned here. For this reason he said, indicating by the omission of the governing verb the constraint of the situation from mentioning it because of the magnitude of the terror and the swiftness of punishment upon touching her with harm, and he increased the honouring (p-82) by repeating the Divine Name: ﴿نَاقَةَ اللَّهِ﴾ "the she-camel of Allah," that is, the Greatest King, to whom all sovereignty belongs entirely, so He does not permit anyone who violates His sanctity and dares against what He has attributed to Himself. For this reason he repeated the explicit noun rather than a pronoun. The governing verb is "leave her" or "beware," or something similar, meaning: beware of harming her in every respect. ﴿وَسُقْيَاهَا﴾ "and her drink," that is, the water which Allah the Exalted appointed for her to drink, and it is her well. So do not keep her away from her well on the day when it is her turn to drink, and do not touch her with harm. It seems that he, upon him be peace, understood after a period of time that they intended to hamstring her, so he repeated the warning to them.

﴿So they denied him.﴾ That is, they committed their denial, because of their rebellion, and this came after his final command in which he warned them of the descent of the punishment. Or the *fa'* may be *fa'* of elucidation (al-fā' al-faṣīḥah), meaning: he said this to them, and then matters arose between him and them concerning it, and they denied him in all of them. ﴿Then they hamstrung her.﴾ That is, because of that denial, some of them did it in deed and some of them by approving of it. ﴿Then He destroyed them.﴾ That is, He punished them with a complete punishment that covered, enveloped, overwhelmed and uprooted them. He crushed their heads with it, hastened to finish them off, and ground them down, with intense anger. Al-Rāzī said: *al-damdamah* is the shaking of a structure until it is overturned. He indicated its severity and comprehensiveness by using the particle of elevation, saying ﴿upon them﴾. He also indicated the severity of the punishment, because of the intensity of the anger, by turning the speech toward mention of the attribute of bounty that they had rejected, for there is no greater anger than from one whose bounty has been rejected. So He said ﴿their Lord﴾, that is, the One who had been good to them, whose goodness had deceived them, and then He cut it off from them, so they became like yesterday that has passed (ka-amsi al-dābir), ﴿because of their sin﴾, that is, because of its cause.

When they were equal in wrongdoing and disbelief, through the hamstringing of the she-camel, some of them in deed and some of them by approval and incitement, He said, as a consequence of that and as a following result: ﴿So He leveled it﴾, that is, the destruction upon them. He made it such that it was as if it were a land, with exceeding levelling, so that nothing remained in it that stood out from anything, just as He leveled the sun by which He swore, and leveled among people in it, and likewise what He swore by after it. So the destruction fell upon their strong as it fell upon their weak, and it spared none of them, and the destruction of none of them preceded the destruction of another. Rather, they were all like a single soul, from the force of the blast and the intensity of the quake, just as they were equal in disbelief and in approving of the hamstringing of the she-camel. Every soul is, to its owner, like the she-camel, concerning which God, glorified is He, has enjoined upon its owner that he tend His blessing in it, so that he purifies it and does not corrupt it. The she-camel is an expression for a mount by which the journey is cut, sensibly or metaphorically, and this is suitable to be meant as the soul by which the obstacles of deeds are crossed. The watering (*al-suqyā*) is that by which the one watered remains alive, and it is suitable to be meant as remembrance and worship. So whoever does not tend the blessing and thank the Bestower has hamstrung her, and thus deserves destruction from Him. And just as He leveled them together in the destruction, He leveled the guided ones together in salvation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 91, verse 15:

﴿And﴾ i.e., while the state is that He does not fear ﴿its consequence﴾ at any time, i.e., their Lord. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and it is supported by the reading of the people of Madinah and Syria with the fa' (fa', indicating consequence) that follows from the destruction (al-damdama) [and the leveling], and so it is written in their copies of the Qur'an. ﴿Its consequence﴾ i.e., the outcome of this destruction and its aftermath. For He is the Most High King in whose grip everything is, not as every punishing king fears, so that he holds back out of concern for consequences. Thus it is known that He, glorified and exalted, raises His friends because they are upon the truth, and lowers His enemies because they are upon falsehood. Therefore, after this, none goes astray except one who is doomed, whose insight is darker than the pitch-black night. The end has returned to the beginning through the oath and its omitted response, which is the disposition of souls upon differing natures, and the advance warning to them of destruction. The oath itself also (is in this sense), for whoever has these awesome acts, in which He made His creation equal [in them], and this firm arrangement, is such that no matter can overpower Him, and He does not fear any consequence. And Allah is the Granter of success toward what is right.
